newsitem.title: UK: Weinstock sees change in smaller GEC units.
newsitem.headline: Weinstock sees change in smaller GEC units.

text.p: Lord Weinstock, the honorary chairman emeritus of British engineering and defence group GEC following his handover of executive power earlier this year, said a number of changes were likely in smaller group units.

In the first of a series of opinion articles in the Financial Times this week, Weinstock said he wanted the 100-year-old General Electric Company Plc to remain at the forefront of UK and European industry 100 years from now.
Looking at the many units which complement its key defence, engineering and telecoms areas he said "there are possiblities for substantial growth through deals of one sort or another".
Although he gave no details of these, he added there were also "a few bits and pieces GEC would be better off without.
"It's not necessarily urgent that they all be got rid of, but it is on the whole desireable," Weinstock said.

Three weeks ago George Simpson, Weinstock's successor as GEC's chief executive, presented 1996 results that included a hefty 160 million stg charge for restructuring business and writing down some industrial division assets prior to disposal.
GEC's smaller activities range from the leading petrol pump maker Gilbarco across medical equipment, including Picker, to distribution, office equipment and printing firm Videojet.
In an interview that concentrated on his 33 years at GEC and how he had sculpted the giant group, Weinstock said he saw no gain for shareholders or GEC's strategy from any break-up move.
"In GEC, every project area has something in common with another...Overseas, it is always a plus that we are GEC in the round, all supporting whichever subsidiary is trying to operate," he reasoned.
Weinstock said he doubted the view of GEC critics who wanted change to make the group more focused, saying "we already wholly focused -- on making money by satisfying our customers needs."
